title: Optimize CPU request path: thread pinning, serialization hot-path, and pool sharding
author: Priya Menon
description: Motivation: CPU-side request path was a persistent bottleneck in multi-tenant workloads where small chat requests dominated QPS. We observed excessive context switches, serialization overhead, and global locks on the KV cache and scheduling path, causing increased p95/p99 token latencies and reduced effective throughput. This PR introduces three coordinated changes to address the problem: 1) refactor request serialization hot-path to a zero-copy approach and move heavy encoding to background worker threads; 2) shard the request thread-pool per NUMA node/socket and add explicit CPU affinity (thread pinning) to reduce cross-socket traffic and cache-coherence churn; 3) replace a global KV-cache mutex with fine-grained sharded locks and a mostly-read lock-free fast-path for cache hits. The description below documents what changed, measurable impact, testing, and rollout notes. Checklist: - [x] microbench and system benchmarks added - [x] unit tests for new serialization and threadpool behavior - [x] perf canary run and smoke tests passed - [x] documented rollout and rollback steps Key changes (high level): - Introduce RequestFrame which references input buffers and only serializes into wire format when absolutely necessary; small requests (<= 1KB) now take the zero-copy fast-path. - Offload heavy encoding (structured output formatting, length-prefixing) to per-NUMA background workers to reduce latency on the IO thread. - New ShardedThreadPool: pool is instantiated per socket/NUMA region with an affinity manager that pins worker threads to cores. - Use a lock-free read-path for KV cache: optimistic read with sequence counters and fallback to per-shard mutex on write/miss. - Add runtime toggles and metrics: serve.cpu.pin_enabled, serve.threadpool.shards, serve.serialization.fastpath_hits. Performance: - Internal perf canary (c5.18x-large equivalent) with mixed chat load: throughput +1.6x, median token latency -12%, p95 token latency -22%, p99 token latency -28% (improvements concentrated on small/short requests). - CPU utilization more stable per-socket vs previous cross-socket tail spikes. Safety and rollout: - Feature gated behind serve.cpu.pin_enabled and can be toggled by route. - Default rollout: enable on non-critical routes for 24h, then expand. - Fallback: disable serve.cpu.pin_enabled to revert to previous pool. Related: ENG-4821 (investigate tail CPU hotspots), ENG-4890 (continuous batching regressions).

review_comments: Ethan Li: Great direction. Two questions: (1) are we confident the zero-copy path is safe when requests mutate buffers after enqueue? Need explicit ownership transfer or copy-on-write. (2) please add a metric for affinity_migrations (how often a task executes on a different core).

Author (Priya): For (1) we introduced RequestFrame::cloneIfMutable(), this performs a cheap clone only when buffer is shared; added a unit test. For (2) added serve.threadpool.affinity_migrations metric and a dashboard tile in perf canary run.
Marcos Alvarez: Nit: prefer sequence counter naming seq_ctr to avoid confusion with existing SeqLock util. Also please add comments around the optimistic-read fast-path explaining ABA assumptions.
Author (Priya): Renamed to seq_ctr and added lengthy comment block explaining the read/write expectations and tests that validate against ABA scenarios.
Sana Kapoor: Can we gate pinning behind node-level config so customers can opt out at route-level? Also ensure we don't degrade CPU overcommit on Dedicated nodes.
Author (Priya): Added per-route override and runtime config serve.threadpool.allow_route_override=false by default. Documented dedicated capacity guidance in rollout notes.
release_notes: Performance: Reduce CPU-side request path overhead by zero-copy serialization, NUMA-aware sharded thread pools, and sharded KV cache optimistic read-path. Expect up to 1.6x throughput on small-request workloads and significantly reduced p95/p99 token latencies. Rollout gated behind runtime flags.
